summary: Extend existing LIFE manual coverage for AFDS components, storage, network and servicing constraints; retain project quantities and source inconsistencies without plan adoption.

topics.label: Autonomous Fluid Discharge System (AFDS)
topics.description: A tank-level-triggered device discharges collected water through an irrigation network without electrical energy. Intervals depend on fog-water supply, tank settings and the network. The source maintenance label SAD is linked by an explicitly curated correspondence. The manual describes discharge pipe, flotation vessel, protection shell and clamping base. Raising/lowering the setting changes the volume accumulated before discharge; cycling depends on supply and network conditions rather than a fixed calendar. Internal installation is compact but less accessible; external installation offers level adjustment and easier access with greater exposure, maintenance and blockage risk. Auxiliary pulse/Wi-Fi monitoring is separate from the unpowered hydraulic trigger. The manual’s method-summary performance and its dated July 2023 table have different counts and denominators and remain separate snapshots.

topics.label: AFDS flotation and discharge trigger
topics.description: The AFDS trigger consists of a discharge pipe, flotation vessel, protective shell and clamping base. The source describes tank filling, vessel flotation, maximum level, discharge start, tank discharge and reset. It operates through buoyancy without an electronic control device. Adjustment changes the amount collected before irrigation; it does not measure a species’ required dose. The manual describes PVC/HDPE fabrication and a separate pulse-meter/Wi-Fi monitoring arrangement. These are source specifications and construction concepts, not a newly validated engineering design or a drone-transfer interface.

topics.label: Restoration water-storage tanks
topics.description: Water tanks buffer supply for restoration areas that are difficult to service. The LIFE manual describes flexible, polyethylene and metal tanks with different installation stability and access requirements. Flexible tanks need a flat protected surface; rigid tanks need stable support, with metal tanks requiring hard ground. Source-described filling and outlet valves are separate from nursery-stock volumes and plant event doses. The manual recommends siting storage to provide gravity flow while matching network pressure, plot demand and refill effort; undersized storage can require frequent servicing. Its flexible-tank capacity is inconsistent between material and cost passages, so no single corrected specification is adopted.

topics.label: Gravity-fed restoration distribution network
topics.description: The LIFE manual routes stored water through main, plot and flexible irrigation pipes, using elevation to generate flow and valves to divide areas with different requirements. Pressure regulators/gauges manage excessive input pressure; fittings maintain leak-tight connections. Source headings specify 40 mm main, 32 mm medium and 19 mm flexible lines, but the prose also prints conflicting centimetre units. Those discrepancies require engineering confirmation rather than silent repair. The manual distinguishes AFDS plots from the described manual-hose network. Neither the shared use of pipes nor a reservoir opening proves compatibility with an aircraft delivery system.

findings.label: AFDS model cost and flow are configuration-specific
findings.text: The manual gives EUR 855 for an AFDS with a 50 mm discharge pipe and stated output 2,000–6,500 L/hour, including tank interconnections but excluding field installation and water meter. Its adjacent summary reports 2,013 planted trees, 86% survival, EUR 115 per surviving tree and “75 L” need per tree. The summary does not state an event count or observation date there; 75 L is not an event dose. The dated 26 July 2023 table elsewhere instead lists 2,082 planted, 0.83 survival and 101.4 L per surviving tree for AFDS. These different scopes are not averaged or treated as direct replication.

findings.label: LIFE storage example is a project-specific water budget
findings.text: The manual’s storage discussion estimates roughly 40 L per plant for the first year, describes about 12.5 L at each of three important irrigations and illustrates 3,000 plants needing at least 120,000 L storage. The text explicitly allows variation with project and water requirements. Three times 12.5 L is 37.5 L, so the stated 40 L is approximate planning language, not an exact normalized event prescription. No species is assigned by this example; it does not authorize a carob dose, refill schedule or working-plan adoption.

findings.label: Storage and network design have servicing and end-of-life costs
findings.text: The manual favours matching storage size, gravity head and irrigation demand so refill and watering effort remain practical. AFDS internal mounting makes maintenance harder; external mounting improves access/level adjustment but adds exposure and blockage risk. Tanks, primary lines and AFDS are described as reusable, while secondary self-regulated drip lines can be difficult to recover on steep terrain. Auxiliary monitoring records number, frequency and volume of discharges; the unpowered hydraulic trigger is distinct from that instrumentation.

browse_groups.label: Water storage, distribution and servicing
browse_groups.maintenance_rule: Preserve project-specific hydraulic configuration, units, dates and quantity denominators. Generic lifecycle phases remain plant-neutral. Storage, daily release, total water and dose are distinct; no plan adoption or untested drone compatibility from shared components.
browse_groups.description: Follow the water chain from storage through a level-triggered AFDS and distribution network to servicing. The LIFE example uses supply-dependent cycles and gravity head; it also documents access, pressure, maintenance and material-recovery limits. Compare this with small planting reservoirs through the refill-access link, retaining their different scale and interfaces. Method-summary outcomes and dated trial tables have different scopes, and printed tank/pipe specifications contain unresolved differences. These examples guide investigation, not a universal plant dose or an automatically compatible drone system.
